_note: Practice question bank for hunter-interview. Every question here is a practice prompt written for this pack: none is a leaked or confirmed real interview question. 'basis' says why it is here: 'official' = the company's own careers page (in 'sources', each read on the 'checked' date) describes this round or this kind of question; 'community' = commonly reported by candidates in public forums and NOT confirmed by the company. Check the source pages again before an interview; processes change by team, level and year.

google-how-we-hire.says: Possible Google Hiring Assessment (workstyle) and role-related assessments such as a coding exercise; one or two shorter recruiter conversations; a panel of interviews over video or in person; the same clear rubrics for every candidate for a role; role-related, open-ended questions and no brainteasers; AI tools are not permitted during interviews. Links Google's own videos, including a mock system design interview.

google-interview-tips.says: Many questions are like 'Tell me about a time when...' or 'How would you approach this situation...?'; use the STAR method; show impact with data ('Accomplished X, as measured by Y, by doing Z'); be ready to discuss ambiguity, working with people and teams (including conflict and influence) and your leadership style; interviewers watch the thought process and ask follow-ups; clarifying questions are fine; come with your own questions; Search and AI are not permitted during interviews.

meta-techscreen.says: The initial software engineering tech screen is a 45-minute conversation with an engineer that assesses technical skills; Meta offers a downloadable Technical Screen Guide on the page.

meta-onsite.says: The full loop is several conversations that assess technical skills and let hiring managers get to know you; Meta offers a downloadable Full Loop Interview Guide with the details.

nvidia-how-we-hire.says: Full-time roles usually have phone interviews, then virtual or in-person interviews with the hiring manager, team members and people from other groups; one-on-one, small group or panel interviews usually last 30 to 60 minutes; technical roles may do a coding exercise, usually in HackerRank on a whiteboard or a laptop NVIDIA provides; an in-person onsite interview is required before an offer; unapproved outside tools such as ChatGPT are not allowed; an optional 15-minute Insider Chat does not affect the decision.

netflix-culture.says: Netflix's culture page: a Dream Team driven by performance and the keeper test; candor and everyday constructive feedback; people over process; context, not control; informed captains who own significant decisions; freedom with responsibility; pay described as personal top of market for the role and location.

amazon-sde2-prep.says: SDE II: online assessment, then a loop of four 55-minute interviews covering technical competencies and Leadership Principles; write syntactically correct code (no pseudocode) that is scalable, robust and well tested, and check edge cases; data structures and algorithms; system design prep; each interviewer usually asks two or three behavioral questions tied to the Leadership Principles; no brain teasers; include metrics; use the STAR method.

amazon-interview-loop.says: In the interview loop you meet current employees one at a time, each assessing different things; one of them may be a Bar Raiser, someone from another team focused on hiring quality; treat every interviewer the same.

amazon-leadership-principles.says: The 16 Leadership Principles: Customer Obsession; Ownership; Invent and Simplify; Are Right, A Lot; Learn and Be Curious; Hire and Develop the Best; Insist on the Highest Standards; Think Big; Bias for Action; Frugality; Earn Trust; Dive Deep; Have Backbone, Disagree and Commit; Deliver Results; Strive to be Earth's Best Employer; Success and Scale Bring Broad Responsibility.

community.says: Commonly reported by candidates. Not published or confirmed by the company. Treat as a guess about format and topics.

google.name: Google

loop.what: Possible Google Hiring Assessment (workstyle) and a role-related assessment such as a coding exercise, before interviews.
One or two shorter phone or video conversations with the recruiter about key skills, the team and your preferences.
Technical interviews where the interviewer watches how you think, asks follow-ups and expects you to clarify. Usually data structures and algorithms in a shared document, about 45 minutes each.
loop.note: The 45 minutes and the shared document are community-reported.

loop.what: Designing a large system out loud, for more experienced roles. Google's own hiring page links a mock system design interview.
loop.note: Which levels get a design round is community-reported.

loop.what: 'Tell me about a time...' and 'How would you approach...' questions on ambiguity, collaboration, conflict and leadership, scored with the same rubric for everyone. Candidates call it the Googleyness and leadership round.

google.rules: AI tools are not permitted during Google interviews (google-how-we-hire, google-interview-tips). Practice with Claude before, never during.

meta.name: Meta

loop.what: A 45-minute technical conversation with an engineer.
Several conversations that assess technical skills and let hiring managers get to know you. Read Meta's downloadable Full Loop Interview Guide for the official breakdown.
Live coding, often two problems in about 45 minutes, at a fast pace.
System design or product architecture for experienced roles: deep architecture discussion.
Past work: impact, conflict, feedback and growth.

meta.rules: Use Meta's own guides from the two prep pages as the source of truth.

nvidia.name: NVIDIA

loop.what: Phone interviews first, then virtual or in-person interviews.
Technical roles may do a coding exercise, usually in HackerRank on a whiteboard or a laptop NVIDIA provides.
Interviews of 30 to 60 minutes with the hiring manager, team members and other groups; an in-person onsite is required before an offer.
Deep questions in the team's area: C++, CUDA and GPU architecture, parallel programming, deep learning systems, hardware.

nvidia.rules: Unapproved outside tools such as ChatGPT are not allowed during NVIDIA interviews (nvidia-how-we-hire).

netflix.name: Netflix

loop.what: Conversations about how you work, measured against the values on Netflix's culture page: judgment, candor, context not control, informed captains, the keeper test.
loop.note: That culture is assessed in dedicated conversations is community-reported; the values themselves are official.

loop.what: Real-world system ownership: designing and operating services at scale.
Practical coding, often closer to real work than puzzles.

netflix.rules: Read the culture page end to end before any Netflix conversation.

amazon.name: Amazon

loop.what: An online assessment before the loop.
Four 55-minute interviews; each interviewer assesses different competencies, technical and Leadership Principles.
Syntactically correct code, no pseudocode; scalable, robust, well-tested; edge cases; data structures and algorithms.
System design for SDE II.
Two or three behavioral questions per interviewer, tied to the Leadership Principles. STAR answers with metrics.
One interviewer may be a Bar Raiser from another team, focused on hiring quality. Treat every interviewer the same.

amazon.rules: Prepare two stories per Leadership Principle, each with a number.

any.name: Any company

loop.what: Past-behavior questions answered with STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result, with a number.
loop.note: Amazon's prep page recommends STAR too (amazon-sde2-prep).

loop.what: Your questions for them at the end. Google's tips page says to come ready with questions.

any.rules: Practice before. Never use Claude during a live interview.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to make a decision without the information you wanted. What did you do, and how did it turn out?
Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate about a technical approach. How did you resolve it?
Tell me about a time you got a group to follow your plan when you were not their manager.
How would you approach a quarter where two partner teams want opposite things from the service you own?
Tell me about the accomplishment you are proudest of, as: accomplished X, as measured by Y, by doing Z.
Tell me about a time you pushed yourself well outside your comfort zone at work.
Tell me about a project with a cross-functional or distributed team. What made it work, and what did you change along the way?
Tell me about a time you changed a teammate's mind with data rather than authority.
Given a stream of request latencies, return the 99th percentile of the last N requests after each new one. Then make it fast when N is a million.
Write a rate limiter that allows at most K requests per user in any rolling minute. How does it change with ten million users?
Given services and their dependencies, return an order to deploy them, or report the cycle that makes it impossible.
Given maintenance windows for many machines, return the time ranges when every machine is up.
Find the shortest route for a packet across a network graph when some links are down, and say what changes if links have different costs.
Implement a cache with a fixed capacity that evicts the least recently used entry, with constant-time get and put.
Design a service that stores and serves configuration for thousands of other services, with safe, gradual rollouts.
Design a global metrics pipeline that collects latency from every server and answers p99 queries within seconds.
Take a system you built and redesign it for a hundred times the traffic. What breaks first, and what do you change?
Design a scheduler that runs batch jobs across a cluster and keeps going when machines fail.
Given a list of friendships, return everyone exactly two connections away from a user, ranked by mutual friends.
Return the K most frequent hashtags in a stream of posts, and keep the answer current as posts arrive.
Can a string become a palindrome if you delete at most one character? Return the index to delete.
Flatten a tree of nested comments into display order, with each comment's depth.
Design a news feed for a billion users.
Design the backend for live comments on a video watched by millions at once.
Design the APIs and data model for uploading photos into shared albums.
Tell me about the project with the most impact you have shipped. How did you measure it?
Tell me about the hardest feedback you have received and what you did with it.
Tell me about a conflict with a coworker that you resolved. What would you do the same way next time?
Tell me about a time you shipped fast with incomplete information. What did you decide not to do?
Explain how a GPU runs thousands of threads at once, and what a warp is.
What is memory coalescing, and why does it matter for a CUDA kernel's speed?
A deep learning training job is slower than expected. Walk through how you find out why, end to end.
In C++, when do move semantics matter, and what do they save?
How would you split a model too large for one GPU across several GPUs for inference?
Implement matrix multiplication, then make it cache-friendly and explain the speedup.
Apply a 3 by 3 blur to a grayscale image using as little extra memory as you can.
Write a thread-safe bounded queue and explain how it avoids deadlock.
Tell me about the hardest technical problem you solved by going back to first principles.

questions.tests: fit with the hiring manager's team
questions.question: Why this team at NVIDIA, and what do you want to be able to do in a year that you cannot do now?
Tell me about a significant decision you made yourself as the person with the most context, without waiting for approval.
Tell me about feedback you gave a peer that was hard to say. How did you say it, and what changed?
Describe a time you had context but no authority. How did you get people aligned without telling them what to do?
Which part of the Netflix culture page do you agree with least, and why?
Tell me about a mistake of yours that affected other people. What did you share, and with whom?
If your manager ran the keeper test on you today, what would they say, and what would you want them to say?
Design a system that chooses which artwork to show each member for each title.
Design playback so it keeps working when an entire cloud region fails.
Build a key-value store that returns the value a key had at any past timestamp.
Tell me about a time you changed a plan because of what a customer actually needed.
Tell me about a time you took on something outside your job because nobody else would.
Tell me about a time you made something much simpler for the people using it.
Tell me about a call you got right when others disagreed, and one you got wrong.
Tell me about something you taught yourself recently and how you used it at work.
Tell me about a time you helped a teammate get noticeably better at their job.
Tell me about a time you would not ship something because it was not good enough.
Tell me about a time you proposed something far bigger than what you were asked for.
Tell me about a time you acted fast with incomplete data. What was the risk, and how did you limit it?
Tell me about a result you got with fewer people, money or time than you wanted.
Tell me about a time you admitted a mistake to your team before anyone else found it.
Tell me about a time a metric looked fine but you dug in and found a real problem.
Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision, said so, and then committed to it fully.
Tell me about a time you hit a hard deadline despite a serious setback.

questions.tests: Strive to be Earth's Best Employer
questions.question: Tell me about something you did that made your team a better place to work.

questions.tests: Success and Scale Bring Broad Responsibility
questions.question: Tell me about a time you weighed the effects of your work on people beyond your team and your users.
From an order log, return the top K products by units sold in the last hour. Write it as production code with tests and edge cases.
Given package weights and a truck limit, return the fewest trucks needed, and prove your approach is right.
Design the classes for a parking garage with small, medium and large spots and a ticketing flow.
Design an order-tracking service that shows customers where their package is right now.
Design a service that sends delivery notifications to millions of customers with no duplicates and no misses.

questions.tests: your story in about a minute
questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
Why this company, and why this team?
Tell me about a project that failed. What would you do differently?
Tell me about a time you had more work than time. How did you choose what to drop?
What is the hardest bug you have fixed? Walk me through how you found it.
Tell me about a production incident you handled. What did you do in the first hour?
Ask them: what would make someone great in this role after six months?
Ask them: what is the hardest problem the team is working on this year?
Ask them: how does the team run design reviews and decide between options?
Ask them: what does on-call look like, and how has it changed in the last year?
